https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: With Putin showing no sign of abandoning his far-reaching territorial demands, even as Russia’s summer offensive stalls, the Kremlin faces a growing manpower headache. Photograph: Igor Ivanko/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen With Putin showing no sign of abandoning his far-reaching territorial demands, even as Russia’s summer offensive stalls, the Kremlin faces a growing manpower headache. Photograph: Igor Ivanko/AFP/Getty Images Russia Putin’s recruiters scramble to avoid second mass mobilisation as Ukraine losses mount Russia is losing 30,000 casualties a month, and the country’s regions are under pressure to feed the ‘meat-grinder’. Experts say it may not be enough Pjotr Sauer Fri 14 Aug 2026 09.00 EDT Last modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 14.10 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google In kitchens and Telegram chats across Russia, the same question is being asked with growing frequency: will Vladimir Putin order another mobilisation? Nearly five years into the war, Russia is scrambling to find enough soldiers to replenish its ranks, as voluntary recruitment slows and its forces suffer heavy losses on the battlefield in Ukraine . With Putin showing no sign of abandoning his far-reaching territorial demands, even as Russia’s summer offensive stalls, the Kremlin faces a growing manpower headache. “The problem for the Kremlin is that it is getting much harder to find people willing to fight, even for crazy money,” said Aleksei Tabalov, a human rights activist and director of an organisation that helps Russian conscripts. Putin last resorted to mobilisation in September 2022, when a series of dramatic battlefield setbacks forced the Kremlin to call up 300,000 reservists to stabilise the front. View image in fullscreen A billboard advertising ‘contract military service’ beside a highway outside Krasnodar, Russia. Photograph: AP Since then, Moscow has avoided another deeply unpopular call-up by relying largely on high paid voluntary contracts to fill the ranks with roughly 1.3 million contract soldiers Russia has recruited since. Men, particularly from Russia’s poorer regions, have been offered life-changing signing bonuses and salaries on open-ended contracts amounting to several years of local wages, alongside substantial payouts to their families if they are killed. But Russia’s heavy losses mean it must continue finding new soldiers at a high rate. Western estimates put Russian casualties at more than 30,000 killed and wounded a month, a toll that reflects the army’s attritional “meat grinder” tactics, in which troops are repeatedly sent forward in small assault groups despite heavy losses. Moscow, meanwhile, now recruits roughly 1,000 soldiers a day, according to calculations by Janis Kluge, a Russia expert at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs, which means most new recruits are used to replenish depleted units rather than expand Russia’s offensive capacity. That has once again raised the prospect of mobilisation. Top Russian officials have dismissed reports of an impending call-up, with former president Dmitry Medvedev describing them as “nonsense” and a “lying provocation” by Ukraine. Two people familiar with discussions in Moscow also said there was no indication that Putin had decided to order another mass mobilisation. A senior western official likewise said there were no signs that a decision had been taken. View image in fullscreen A firefighting helicopter drops water over a food warehouse damaged during Russian drone strikes near Kyiv, 12 August 2026. Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/Reuters But fears that another call-up may be on the way have nevertheless increasingly entered everyday conversations. In Telegram chats used by local sports teams, work colleagues and groups of friends, Russians swap rumours about a possible mobilisation and share advice on securing exemptions or avoiding the draft. Some speculate that a new call-up could come after September’s elections to the Duma. “It’s guesswork right now whether mobilisation will actually happen,” said Ivan Chuviliaev, a spokesperson for Get Lost, a group that helps Russian soldiers desert. But he said the renewed speculation was already being exploited to boost recruitment. “The panic around mobilisation is being used by officials to pressure men into signing contracts,” Chuviliaev said. “The message is: mobilisation is coming anyway, so you might as well sign a contract now and get a payout before you’re forced to fight.” View image in fullscreen Putin recently signed a law expanding the pool of convicted prisoners eligible to sign contracts with the army. Photograph: Russian President official/APAImages/Shutterstock For now, people familiar with the Kremlin’s thinking say the authorities appear determined to strong-arm more men into signing contracts rather than risk another mobilisation. Over the summer, lawyers and activists have documented increasingly coercive recruitment tactics in several regions, with men detained on the street by police, taken from workplaces or summoned to stations – before being brought to military recruitment offices and pressed to sign contracts. “It has turned into a hunt for people,” said Tabalov. “Under various pretexts, through deception, blackmail, violence and threats, they are forcing them to sign contracts.” Tabalov said recruiters were increasingly targeting what he described as “socially marginalised” men, including those with debts, criminal cases or other vulnerabilities that could be used to put pressure on them to enlist. In the southern Penza region, where some of the most aggressive draft methods have been reported, videos posted online have shown men being driven away in vans as relatives protested outside recruitment offices. Activists say some have been threatened with prosecution or beaten until they agreed to sign. The search has widened elsewhere too. Universities, technical colleges and vocational schools have been encouraged to recruit students into newly formed drone units, offering another source of manpower for the military. Putin recently signed a law expanding the pool of convicted prisoners eligible to sign contracts with the army, including people convicted of “serious and especially serious crimes”. Much of the responsibility for finding soldiers has been pushed down to Russia’s regions. Governors and local administrations are expected to meet recruitment targets set by Moscow, giving the Kremlin some distance from the drive while leaving regional officials responsible for finding enough men in their own territories. Around that system, a lucrative recruitment industry has emerged. Regional governments offer thousands of dollars not only to soldiers who sign contracts but also to those who find them, with “bring a friend” schemes paying residents for every person they persuade to enlist. View image in fullscreen Smoke rises from an oil refinery after a Ukrainian drone attack in Moscow, 18 June 2026. Photograph: Social Media/Reuters Private recruiters and public-sector employees scour social media for candidates, while advertisements for military contracts have become ubiquitous online. Russian regions have paid recruiters at least 7.7bn roubles ($96m) since such schemes were introduced, according to the independent Russian outlet IStories . One recruiter in central Russia, speaking to the Guardian on condition of anonymity, said his organisation was expected to find between 20 and 30 men each month, with bonuses for exceeding the target and penalties for falling short. “It was easier last year,” the recruiter said. “Now it is getting harder.” The recruiter said mobilisation was also being discussed in his office, but that there had been no orders or indications that a new draft was imminent. Another mass call-up, however, would carry significant political risks for the Kremlin. The 2022 call-up triggered one of the biggest episodes of domestic disruption since the invasion began, prompting a mass exodus of Russians and a sharp drop in Putin’s approval ratings. It would also come at a potentially sensitive moment. Recent polling suggests confidence in the course of the war is weakening, with the share of Russians who believe the campaign in Ukraine is going well falling to its lowest level since April 2022. For now, analysts say Moscow is more likely to step up recruitment efforts through higher bonuses, pressure on regional officials and increasingly coercive tactics. Whether that will be enough could ultimately determine if Putin resorts to another mobilisation, said Tabalov, the activist. The options before the Kremlin, Tabalov said, could range from another mass call-up to a more selective mobilisation, sending existing conscripts to the front or quietly calling up reservists for frontline service. “I don’t think they’ll be able to recruit enough people under the current system,” Tabalov said. “Then they’ll be faced with the question of what form mobilisation should take.” Explore more on these topics Russia Ukraine Vladimir Putin Europe news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://www.politico.eu/article/germany-.text: NEW YORK — German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul held a surprise meeting with his Russian counterpart Sergey Lavrov at the U.N. on Saturday, just one day after he welcomed the U.S. invite for Russian President Vladimir Putin to the G20 summit. "It was an intense conversation", Wadephul told German public television ZDF after the meeting, which lasted about 30 minutes. "Of course, we did not reach agreement on key points. It was important to me to make it clear that Germany does not accept incidents such as the drone attack in Leipzig, and that this is an escalation that is unacceptable. And I clearly warned Russia not to continue down this path. We can defend ourselves, we can fight back. And that's exactly what we'll do." “Wadephul called on the Russian Federation to abandon its dangerous path of escalation toward Germany, Europe, and NATO,” a German official said after the meeting. The official was granted anonymity to discuss the meeting. Advertisement Advertisement The minister also “condemned Russia’s ongoing and increasingly targeted aggression against the Ukrainian civilian population” and highlighted that, “every month, tens of thousands of Russian soldiers die in a hopeless war of attrition, while the Russian economy continues to collapse,” the official said. The meeting of the German and the Russian ministers — the first of that kind since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 — comes amid high tensions between Berlin and Moscow. Earlier this month, the German government accused Russian intelligence services of having orchestrated the attempted drone attack on a Ukrainian cargo plane at the Leipzig airport in Eastern Germany. In reaction, Germany imposed sanctions, including the closure of Russia's consulate in Bonn, to which Moscow responded with similar measures against Germany, notably the closure of Germany's consulate in St. Petersburg. Germany and Russia also clashed during a U.N. Security Council meeting earlier this week, during which Wadephul slammed “Russia's reckless and dangerous escalation in Europe,” while Lavrov accused Europe of “criminal methods.” The German official said that Wadephul “made clear” during Saturday's meeting “that incidents such as the recent attempted attack in Leipzig or other hybrid attacks would not shake Germany’s determination to support Ukraine, which is under attack. However, they would further damage bilateral relations with Germany, which have already been severely strained by Russia.” The Russian side did not immediately provide a detailed readout of Saturday's meeting. Moscow's foreign ministry spokesperson, Maria Zakharova, instead referred to a polemic Russian report that calls into question the authenticity of the Bucha massacre, and that appears to have been put on the table during the ministers' meeting. Advertisement Advertisement The meeting was also immediately overshadowed by different explanations over who had requested it. Zakharova claimed that Wadephul had asked to meet Lavrov. Yet Wadephul told ZDF that he had agreed to meet Lavrov after the Russian foreign minister, through third-party intermediaries, signaled a willingness to engage in talks. The reunion of Wadephul and Lavrov was held against the backdrop of renewed efforts by the U.S. and its Western allies to jumpstart peace talks between Russia and Ukraine. Earlier this week, the U.S. government issued an invitation to Putin for the G20 summit in Miami in December, raising the possibility of potential negotiations between the Russian president and his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Florida. While some other European leaders criticized that invitation, Wadephul said he welcomed the initiative , calling it "a litmus test for Putin." “Opportunities like this must be seized,” Wadephul said on Friday. Wadephul had added a caveat, however, saying that, “in my view, a ceasefire is also necessary in order to be able to negotiate in earnest.” This article was updated with Wadephul's comments to ZDF.
